title: Change control in linear vs iterative life cycles
blurb: Explain where each change control stage plays out differently in linear and iterative life cycles, and when an iterative project still needs the formal route.
question: Millbrook Station's building works follow a linear life cycle, while its passenger app is built in fixed two-week iterations. The operator asks for a platform 2 lift on the building and a live-departures screen in the app. How will the two requests be handled differently, and why?

teach.h: What is fixed decides how change is handled
teach.body: In a linear life cycle the SCOPE is defined and baselined up front, so any change to that baselined scope goes through the formal change control process, and time and cost move only through it. In an iterative life cycle TIME and COST are fixed while scope flexes. So most scope changes are absorbed by the product owner re-prioritising the backlog between iterations. Formal change control is kept for changes to the fixed time or cost, or to the overall objectives.

rows.label: Flexes
values: Time and cost, via change control

teach.caption: Both control change. They differ in what is protected and who holds the decision for scope.

teach.h: The six stages in each life cycle
head: Stage
Linear
Iterative
teach.caption: A typical way the stages play out. In iterative work they are lighter and faster, but the same logic applies: understand it, decide it, plan it, then build it.
New requests normally wait for the next time box: the current one is not disturbed. Adding an item means something of lower priority drops.

teach.body: The building works are linear. The operator's request for a platform 2 lift becomes CR-031, is evaluated by specialists and goes to the sponsor, because it changes the baselined scope, cost and dates. The passenger app is iterative. The operator's request for a live-departures screen becomes a backlog item; the product owner rates it a Should have and swaps out a Could have, so the launch date and budget hold. Later the operator asks to launch the app six weeks early. That changes a fixed constraint, so it goes through formal change control.

root.label: A change arrives
root.sub: Does it alter fixed time, cost or objectives?

teach.caption: Most changes on an iterative project take the left branch. The right branch is the formal six-stage process.
Neither approach lets change drift in uncontrolled.

teach.body: Linear change control gives strong control, predictability and a clear audit trail, which suits regulated work and physical builds where late change is costly. Its downside is that it is slower and change late in the life cycle is expensive. Iterative handling responds quickly and cheaply to new learning, but it needs a committed, disciplined product owner, makes total scope harder to forecast and can drift without discipline. A hybrid project uses both, so it needs a clear rule on which route each change takes.

teach.text: Two classic traps. 'Iterative projects have no change control' is wrong: scope changes are controlled through the prioritised backlog, and changes to fixed time, cost or objectives still go through formal change control. 'In iterative work, a change is added to the current time box straight away' is also wrong: it normally waits for the next iteration, and something of lower priority comes out.

teach.h: How this comes up in a written answer
items: State what is fixed: scope in linear; time and cost in iterative.
Linear: scope changes go through the formal process (request to implement) with the sponsor or change authority deciding.
Iterative: most scope changes are new backlog items, prioritised by the product owner between iterations.
Iterative still uses formal change control for changes to fixed time, cost or overall objectives.
Give a trade-off: control and predictability versus speed and responsiveness.
Linear: scope is baselined, so changes to it go through formal change control.
Iterative: time and cost are fixed, so most scope changes are absorbed by re-prioritising the backlog.
The product owner prioritises between iterations; the current time box is protected.
Iterative projects still use formal change control for time, cost or objectives.
Hybrid projects need a clear rule on which route a change takes.

summary: You can now explain how each change control stage differs between linear and iterative life cycles, and why: linear protects a scope baseline, iterative protects time and cost. You can also say when an iterative project must still use formal change control.

A.q: In an iterative life cycle, how are most changes to scope normally handled?
options: By a formal request to the change board
By extending the current time box
By re-prioritising the product backlog
By rebaselining the whole project plan
A.why: With time and cost fixed, scope flexes: the product owner adds the change to the backlog and re-prioritises it between iterations.

whyNot.0: The formal route is kept for changes to fixed time, cost or objectives, not routine scope changes.
whyNot.1: Time boxes are fixed; extending them defeats the point of the approach.
whyNot.3: Full rebaselining is the linear response to a scope change.

A.q: In a linear life cycle, what happens to a proposed change to the baselined scope?
options: It goes through formal change control
The product owner swaps it with an item
It joins the next time box automatically
The team agrees it informally on site
A.why: In linear projects the scope is baselined, so changes to it go through the formal change control process.

whyNot.1: Swapping items in a backlog is how an iterative project handles most scope change.
whyNot.2: Linear projects do not plan in time boxes, and nothing joins the plan without a decision.
whyNot.3: Informal agreement bypasses evaluation and authority: uncontrolled change.

A.q: On an iterative project, who normally decides the priority of a newly requested feature?
options: The project sponsor
The development team
The quality manager
The product owner
A.why: The product owner owns the backlog and decides the priority of new items between iterations.

whyNot.0: The sponsor is involved when a change affects fixed time, cost or objectives, not routine prioritisation.
whyNot.1: The team estimates effort but the product owner sets priority.
whyNot.2: A quality manager is concerned with standards, not backlog priority.

B.q: An online retailer is building a new checkout in two-week sprints, with a fixed budget and launch date. Marketing asks for a gift-wrap option, rated a Should have, which fits if a Could have is dropped. What is the most appropriate action?
options: Send a formal change request to the project sponsor
Product owner adds it and reorders the backlog
Add it to the sprint already under way
Reject it, because the scope is now fixed
B.why: The change fits within the fixed time and cost by swapping priorities, so it is handled by the product owner through the backlog.

whyNot.0: Time, cost and objectives are unaffected, so the formal route is not needed.
whyNot.2: The current sprint is protected; new items wait for the next one.
whyNot.3: In iterative work scope is the flexible element, not the fixed one.

B.q: The same retailer's board now asks for the checkout to launch six weeks earlier than agreed. How should this be handled?
options: The product owner drops low-priority items
The team simply works shorter sprints
Leave it until the final sprint review
Formal change control, as time is fixed
B.why: The launch date is one of the fixed constraints, so changing it goes through formal change control with the sponsor or change authority.

whyNot.0: Dropping items may be part of the response, but changing a fixed date needs a formal decision first.
whyNot.1: Changing the sprint pattern does not deal with a change to an agreed constraint.
whyNot.2: Waiting removes any chance of assessing and planning the earlier date properly.

B.q: Which statement about change control on iterative projects is correct?
options: Formal control still covers time and cost
There is no change control at all
Each new user story needs sponsor sign-off
Changes join the current time box at once
B.why: Iterative projects control scope through the backlog, and keep formal change control for changes to fixed time, cost or objectives.

whyNot.1: Change is controlled, through the prioritised backlog and the formal route when needed.
whyNot.2: Routine stories are prioritised by the product owner, not signed off by the sponsor.
whyNot.3: The current time box is normally protected; new items wait for the next.

C.q: Which TWO describe change control in a linear life cycle rather than an iterative one? 1. Changes are measured against a detailed scope baseline 2. The product owner reorders the backlog 3. Scope changes use a change log and a change authority 4. Scope flexes within fixed time boxes
options: 1 and 2
2 and 4
1 and 3
3 and 4
C.why: Linear projects baseline the scope in detail (1) and route scope changes through the change log and a change authority (3). Items 2 and 4 describe iterative working.

whyNot.0: Backlog reordering by a product owner (2) is iterative.
whyNot.3: Scope flexing within fixed time boxes (4) is iterative.

C.q: A hospital is building a new wing (linear) and a patient app (iterative). Clinicians ask for an extra screen in the app, which fits the next time box, and an extra operating theatre in the wing. How should the two requests be handled?
options: Both through formal change control
App: backlog; wing: change control
App: change control; wing: backlog
Both added to the app's backlog
C.why: The app screen fits within fixed time and cost, so the product owner prioritises it in the backlog. The theatre changes the wing's baselined scope, so it needs formal change control.

whyNot.0: The app screen does not affect fixed time, cost or objectives, so the backlog is the right route.
whyNot.2: This reverses the routes: the linear wing needs formal control, the iterative app does not.
whyNot.3: A building has no backlog; a change to its baselined scope needs formal control.

C.q: Why does a linear life cycle rely on a formal route for scope changes?
options: Linear projects never allow scope change
Time and cost are fixed, so scope can't flex
Users review the product every iteration
Late change is costly once scope is fixed
C.why: Linear projects baseline the scope early and build on it, so changing it later can mean costly rework. A formal route makes sure the impact is understood first.

whyNot.0: Scope can change in linear projects; it just goes through change control.
whyNot.1: Fixed time and cost with flexing scope describes iterative, not linear.
whyNot.2: Feedback every iteration is a feature of iterative life cycles.

reteach.title: A restaurant's set menu vs its specials board
reteach.question: A restaurant has a printed set menu for a wedding party and a chalk specials board for walk-in diners. A customer asks for something new on each. Why are the two requests handled so differently?

blocks.body: The wedding menu was agreed and costed months ago, with ingredients ordered. Changing it means checking cost, supplier, timing and the couple's approval: a formal route, like linear change control. The specials board changes daily: the chef has a fixed kitchen and budget each day and simply picks what goes on it, wiping off something less popular to make room, like an iterative backlog. But if the owner wanted to open an extra evening, that changes the fixed time and cost, so it needs a proper decision.

blocks.h: Two ways to handle a new request

blocks.text: The specials board is still controlled: the chef decides, and only between services. Iterative does not mean uncontrolled.

explain.body: Linear: scope is fixed by a detailed baseline; time and cost change only through change control. Iterative: time and cost are fixed (each time box and the overall budget); scope flexes by priority, while quality is protected.

test.q: In an iterative life cycle, which elements are treated as fixed?
options: Time and cost
Scope and time
Scope and cost
Scope only
test.why: Iterative life cycles fix time and cost and let scope flex according to priority.

whyNot.1: Scope is the flexible element in iterative work.
whyNot.2: Scope flexes; cost is fixed alongside time.
whyNot.3: Fixing scope is the linear approach.

explain.body: Linear: a change request is raised and logged, the PM screens it, then specialists assess its impact. Iterative: the request becomes a new backlog item; the product owner reviews and refines it, and the team sizes its value and effort, usually in backlog refinement.

test.q: On an iterative project, what usually takes the place of a formal initial evaluation of a new scope request?
options: A monthly meeting of the change board
An audit by the project assurance team
The product owner refining the backlog
A full rebaselining of the project plan
test.why: The product owner reviews and refines new items in the backlog, which serves the screening purpose of an initial evaluation.

whyNot.0: A change board is the formal linear-style route, kept for time, cost or objectives.
whyNot.1: Assurance checks the process; it does not screen individual backlog items.
whyNot.3: Rebaselining is a linear response to an approved change.

explain.body: Linear: the sponsor or change authority approves, rejects or defers, then the baseline, PMP and configuration records are updated. Iterative: the product owner prioritises the item; the backlog is reordered and the next time box is planned, so a lower-priority item may drop out.

test.q: On an iterative project, what does 'update plans' typically involve after a new item is prioritised?
options: Re-approving the whole of the business case
Reordering the backlog and next time box
Moving the fixed release date later
Raising a new version of the contract
test.why: The backlog is reordered and the next time box is planned around the new priorities.

whyNot.0: A routine scope swap does not require the business case to be re-approved.
whyNot.2: The release date is fixed; moving it would need formal change control.
whyNot.3: Routine prioritisation does not change the contract.

explain.h: When iterative still needs the formal route
explain.body: If a change would alter the fixed time (a release date), the fixed cost (the budget) or the overall objectives, the product owner cannot absorb it by swapping priorities. It goes through formal change control to the sponsor or change authority.

test.q: Which change on an iterative project would most clearly need formal change control?
options: Swapping two Could have stories
Splitting a large story into two
Rewording a story's acceptance test
Moving the agreed release date
test.why: The release date is a fixed constraint, so changing it needs a formal decision by the sponsor or change authority.

whyNot.0: Swapping priorities is routine backlog management.
whyNot.1: Splitting stories is normal refinement by the team and product owner.
whyNot.2: Clarifying acceptance criteria is routine refinement within the backlog.
